row.subject: Science
row.questionText: How does chemical coordination take place in animals?
row.answer: Chemical coordination in animals occurs through hormones secreted by endocrine glands. Hormones are released directly into the bloodstream and carried to target organs, where they bind to specific receptors and produce a response. This system is slower than nervous coordination but reaches all cells.
solutionSteps: Endocrine glands (pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, etc.) secrete hormones.
Hormones travel in blood to specific target organs/tissues.
They bind to target cell receptors and elicit a response (e.g., insulin lowers blood sugar).
Feedback mechanism regulates hormone secretion.
row.finalAnswer: Endocrine glands secrete hormones → carried in blood → act on target organs.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: How does chemical coordination take place in animals?
row.answer: Chemical coordination in animals is via hormones secreted by endocrine glands. Hormones are released directly into blood, transported to target organs where they bind to specific receptors and produce a response. Examples: thyroxin from thyroid (metabolism), insulin from pancreas (blood sugar), adrenaline from adrenal (fight-or-flight), growth hormone from pituitary (body growth), testosterone/oestrogen from gonads (puberty). Hormone levels are regulated by feedback mechanisms — e.g., rising blood sugar triggers insulin release; falling sugar reduces it.
solutionSteps: Endocrine glands secrete hormones — pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads.
Hormones are released into the bloodstream.
They travel to target organs/cells with specific receptors.
Binding triggers a response (e.g., insulin → glucose uptake).
Feedback mechanisms regulate hormone levels (negative feedback).
Example: blood sugar rises → pancreas releases insulin → sugar drops → insulin reduces.
row.finalAnswer: Endocrine glands secrete hormones → carried in blood → act on target organs; regulated by feedback.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: Draw the structure of a neuron and explain its function.
row.answer: A neuron has three main parts: (1) Cell body (cyton) — contains nucleus and cytoplasm; (2) Dendrites — short branches that receive impulses from other neurons or receptors; (3) Axon — long fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body. Functions: dendrites pick up stimuli → impulse passes to cell body → travels along axon → at axonal end, chemical (neurotransmitter) is released across synapse to next neuron or to muscle/gland.
solutionSteps: Draw labelled neuron showing: dendrites (input), cell body with nucleus, axon (long, may be myelinated), axon terminals, synapse.
Dendrites: receive electrical signals from other neurons or sensory receptors.
Cell body: integrates incoming signals; contains nucleus and most organelles.
Axon: conducts the electrical impulse away from cell body towards axon terminal.
Axon terminal: releases neurotransmitter chemicals into synapse.
Synapse: chemical crosses gap → generates new impulse in next neuron or triggers muscle/gland response.
row.finalAnswer: Neuron = dendrites + cell body + axon; carries impulses from receptors to effectors via synapses.
row.strategyHint: REQUIRES-FIGURE: must draw labelled neuron diagram.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational, given that √5 is irrational.
row.answer: Assume, to the contrary, that 3 + 2√5 is rational. Then we can write 3 + 2√5 = a/b for some integers a, b with b ≠ 0. Rearranging: 2√5 = a/b − 3 = (a − 3b)/b. Dividing by 2: √5 = (a − 3b)/(2b). Since a, b are integers, (a − 3b)/(2b) is a ratio of two integers with non-zero denominator, hence is rational. So √5 would be rational. But we are given that √5 is irrational — contradiction. Therefore our assumption was wrong, and 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Suppose, for contradiction, that 3 + 2√5 is rational. Then 3 + 2√5 = a/b with a, b integers, b ≠ 0.
Isolate √5: 2√5 = a/b − 3 = (a − 3b)/b.
Divide by 2: √5 = (a − 3b)/(2b).
RHS is a ratio of integers (with non-zero denominator) → rational.
So √5 would be rational, contradicting the fact that √5 is irrational. Hence 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
row.strategyHint: Isolate √5 on one side; show RHS is rational; contradict.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: Prove that √2 is an irrational number.
solutionSteps: Assume, to the contrary, that √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b for some coprime integers a, b (b ≠ 0). So b√2 = a; squaring: 2b² = a².
Thus 2 divides a², so 2 divides a. Write a = 2c for some integer c. Substitute: 2b² = 4c² ⇒ b² = 2c². So 2 divides b², hence 2 divides b.
So both a and b are divisible by 2 — contradicting that a and b are coprime. The assumption is wrong, therefore √2 is irrational.

row.subject: Maths
row.question: Prove that √2 is an irrational number.
row.answer: Assume √2 is rational, i.e., √2 = p/q in lowest terms. Squaring gives 2 = p²/q² ⇒ p² = 2q², so p² is even and hence p is even. Let p = 2k. Then 2q² = 4k² ⇒ q² = 2k², so q is also even. This contradicts the assumption that p/q is in lowest terms. Hence √2 is irrational.
solutionSteps: Assume √2 is rational, so √2 = p/q where p and q are coprime integers, q ≠ 0.; Squaring both sides: 2 = p²/q². [1]
So p² = 2q², hence p² is even and p is even. Let p = 2k; then 2q² = (2k)² = 4k² ⇒ q² = 2k², so q² is even and q is also even. [1]
Then p and q have a common factor 2, which contradicts that p and q are coprime. Therefore our assumption is wrong and √2 is irrational. [1]
row.explanation: This is the classic 3-mark proof-by-contradiction question on irrational numbers. Boards often ask for √2, √3 or similar proofs.

row.questionText: Differentiate between binary fission and multiple fission with one example each.
row.answer:
Binary fission: parent cell splits into two almost equal halves, e.g., Amoeba.
Multiple fission: parent cell divides into many daughter cells at once, e.g., Plasmodium.
row.explanation: Key difference is number of daughter cells produced in one division.
solutionSteps: Binary fission is a type of asexual reproduction where the parent cell divides into two approximately equal daughter cells.; An example of an organism that reproduces by binary fission is Amoeba. [½]
Multiple fission is an asexual reproduction method where the parent cell divides into many daughter cells simultaneously. [½]
An example of an organism that reproduces by multiple fission is Plasmodium. [1]
row.finalAnswer:
Binary fission: parent cell splits into two almost equal halves, e.g., Amoeba.
Multiple fission: parent cell divides into many daughter cells at once, e.g., Plasmodium.

row.questionText: The product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is always:
row.explanation: If r ≠ 0 is rational and x is irrational, then r·x is always irrational. Proof by contradiction: if r·x = q (rational), then x = q/r, which is rational (ratio of two rationals) — contradicting x being irrational. So the product must be irrational.
solutionSteps: Let r be non-zero rational and x be irrational
Assume r·x = q (rational), then x = q/r = rational — contradiction
So r·x must be irrational

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: The product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number is:
row.explanation: If r ≠ 0 is rational and x is irrational, their product r·x is always irrational. Proof: assume r·x = q (rational) → x = q/r, a ratio of two rationals, which would be rational — contradiction. Note: if r = 0, then 0 × (irrational) = 0, which is rational, but the question specifies r is non-zero.
solutionSteps: Let 'r' be a non-zero rational number and 'i' be an irrational number.
Assume, for contradiction, that their product 'ri' is rational.
Then, i = (ri)/r. Since 'ri' and 'r' are rational, their quotient 'i' must also be rational.
This contradicts our initial assumption that 'i' is an irrational number. Hence, the product 'ri' must be irrational.

row.questionText: The sum of a two-digit number and the number obtained by reversing the digits is 66. If the digits of the number differ by 2, find the number.
solutionSteps: Let tens digit = x, units = y; Number = 10x + y, Reversed = 10y + x [1]
(10x+y) + (10y+x) = 66 → 11(x+y) = 66 → x+y = 6; x − y = 2 (given digits differ by 2) [1]

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: The sum of a two-digit number and the number obtained by reversing the digits is 66. If the digits of the number differ by 2, find the number. How many such numbers are there?
row.answer: There are TWO such numbers: 24 and 42. Let the digits be x (tens) and y (units). Then the number is 10x + y and the reversed number is 10y + x. Their sum is 11(x + y) = 66 → x + y = 6. The digits differ by 2: either x − y = 2 or y − x = 2. Case 1 (x − y = 2): x = 4, y = 2 → number = 42. Case 2 (y − x = 2): x = 2, y = 4 → number = 24.
solutionSteps: Let the tens digit = x and units digit = y. Number = 10x + y; reversed = 10y + x.
Digit difference condition: x − y = 2 …(2a) OR y − x = 2 …(2b).
Case 1: (1) and (2a) → 2x = 8 → x = 4, y = 2 → number = 42.
Case 2: (1) and (2b) → 2y = 8 → y = 4, x = 2 → number = 24. Hence two numbers exist: 42 and 24.
row.finalAnswer: Two numbers — 42 and 24 (both satisfy the conditions).
row.strategyHint: Two-digit number value = 10·(tens) + (units); 'differ by 2' has two cases (±).

row.questionText: If the points A(6, 1), B(8, 2), C(9, 4) and D(p, 3) are the vertices of a parallelogram, taken in order, find the value of p.
row.answer: In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so midpoint of AC = midpoint of BD. Midpoint of AC = ((6+9)/2, (1+4)/2) = (15/2, 5/2). Midpoint of BD = ((8+p)/2, (2+3)/2) = ((8+p)/2, 5/2). Equating x-coordinates: 15/2 = (8+p)/2 ⇒ 15 = 8 + p ⇒ p = 7.
solutionSteps: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other ⇒ mid(AC) = mid(BD).
Equate x: 15/2 = (8+p)/2 → p = 7. (y already matches.)
row.strategyHint: For a parallelogram with vertices in order, midpoints of diagonals are equal.

row.questionText: In the given figure, a circle is inscribed in a quadrilateral ABCD in which ∠B = 90°. If AD = 23 cm, AB = 29 cm and DS = 5 cm, find the radius (r) of the circle.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact, so ∠OPB = ∠OQB = 90°. With ∠B = 90° and OP = OQ = r, quadrilateral OQBP is a square.
[1 mark] Tangents from an external point are equal: DR = DS = 5 cm and AQ = AR. Then AR = AD − DR = 23 − 5 = 18 cm, so AQ = 18 cm.
[1 mark] BQ = AB − AQ = 29 − 18 = 11 cm. Since OQBP is a square, radius OQ = BQ = 11 cm.
row.diagramDescription: A circle with centre O inscribed in quadrilateral ABCD with ∠B = 90°. The circle touches the four sides at points P (on AB), Q (on BC), R (on AD) and S (on DC). AD = 23 cm, AB = 29 cm, DS = 5 cm; OP and OQ are radii to the contact points on AB and BC.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: A circle is inscribed in a quadrilateral ABCD in which ∠B = 90°. If AD = 23 cm, AB = 29 cm and DS = 5 cm, find the radius r of the circle.
solutionSteps: From tangent lengths from external point: DR = DS = 5 cm; AR = AD − DR = 23 − 5 = 18 cm. AQ = AR = 18 cm; QB = AB − AQ = 29 − 18 = 11 cm.
In quadrilateral OQBP: ∠B = 90° and ∠OQB = ∠OPB = 90° (tangent-radius). So OQBP is a square with side OQ = OP = r. Hence r = QB = 11 cm.
row.strategyHint: REQUIRES-FIGURE: inscribed circle in quadrilateral with right angle at B.

solutionSteps: Join OQ. OA = OQ, so ∠OQA = ∠OAQ = 30°; exterior angle ∠BOQ = 30° + 30° = 60°.
OB = OQ, so ∠OBQ = ∠OQB = 60°; OQ ⊥ PQ gives ∠BQP = 90° − 60° = 30°.
In ΔOQP: ∠OPQ = 180° − 90° − 60° = 30°. So ∠BQP = ∠BPQ = 30°, hence BP = BQ.

row.questionText: A round table cover has six equal designs as shown in figure. If the radius of the cover is 28 cm, find the cost of making the designs at the rate of ₹0.35 per cm². (Use √3 = 1.7)
solutionSteps: The cover is divided into 6 equilateral triangles by radii; Central angle per sector = 60°; Area of each sector = (60/360) × (22/7) × 28² = (1/6) × 2464 = 410.67 cm² [1]
Area of equilateral triangle = (√3/4) × 28² = (1.7/4) × 784 = 333.2 cm²; Area of each design (segment) = 410.67 − 333.2 = 77.47 cm² [1]

pending_fix_fields.questionText: A round table cover of radius 28 cm has six equal designs. Each design is a minor segment of the circle cut off by a chord that subtends an angle of 60° at the centre (the six chords form a regular hexagon inscribed in the circle). Find the cost of making the designs at the rate of ₹0.35 per cm². (Use π = 22/7 and √3 = 1.7)
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Area of each sector of angle 60° = (60/360) × (22/7) × 28² = 1232/3 ≈ 410.67 cm².
[1 mark] Each chord forms an equilateral triangle with the radii: area = (√3/4) × 28² = (1.7/4) × 784 = 333.2 cm². Area of each design (segment) = 410.67 − 333.2 = 77.47 cm².
[1 mark] Total area of 6 designs = 6 × 77.47 ≈ 464.8 cm²; Cost = 464.8 × 0.35 ≈ ₹162.68.

solutionSteps: [1 mark] Pipe radius = 7 cm = 0.07 m; water speed = 15 km/h = 15000 m/h.
[1 mark] Volume of water per hour = (22/7)(0.07)²(15000) = 231 m³.
[1 mark] Required volume in pond = 50 × 44 × 0.21 = 462 m³.
[1 mark] Time = 462 / 231.
[1 mark] = 2 hours.

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: A vessel is in the form of a hollow hemisphere mounted by a hollow cylinder. The diameter of the hemisphere is 14 cm and the total height of the vessel is 13 cm. Find the inner surface area of the vessel. (Take π = 22/7.)
solutionSteps: Radius r = 14/2 = 7 cm. Height of cylindrical part h = 13 − 7 = 6 cm.
Inner SA = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cylinder = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h).
row.strategyHint: Cylinder height = total height − hemisphere radius; only inner curved surfaces are counted (vessel is hollow, top open).

row.subject: Maths
row.questionText: A box contains 90 discs numbered 1 to 90. If one disc is drawn at random, find the probability that it bears (i) a two-digit number, (ii) a perfect square, (iii) a number divisible by 5.
solutionSteps: Total outcomes = 90.
(i) Two-digit numbers from 10 to 90 → 81 outcomes. P = 81/90 = 9/10.
(iii) Multiples of 5 from 5 to 90: 5, 10, …, 90. Count = 90/5 = 18. P = 18/90 = 1/5.

row.questionText:
Which of the following are combination reactions?
(i) 2KClO₃ --Heat--> 2KCl + 3O₂
(ii) MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂
(iii) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
(iv) Zn + FeSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Fe
solutionSteps: (i) Single reactant breaks down → decomposition. Not combination.
(ii) MgO + H₂O → Mg(OH)₂ — two substances combine to give one product → combination ✓.
(iii) 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ — two elements combine to give one compound → combination ✓.
(iv) Zn displaces Fe from FeSO₄ → displacement. Not combination.
Answer: (d) (ii) and (iii).

row.subject: Science
row.questionText: What are the changes seen in girls at the time of puberty?
row.answer: Changes in girls at puberty: (i) breast size increases with darkening of nipple area; (ii) onset of menstruation; (iii) growth of thick hair in armpits and pubic region; (iv) skin becomes oily, may develop pimples; (v) widening of hips; (vi) increase in height and weight; (vii) increased self-awareness and emotional changes.
solutionSteps: Caused by secretion of oestrogen from ovaries.
Physical: breast development, darkening of nipple area.
Reproductive: onset of menstruation (menarche).
Hair: growth in armpits, pubic area.
Skin: oily, pimples may develop.
Skeletal: widening of hips, growth in height.
row.finalAnswer: Breast development, menstruation onset, hair growth, oily skin, widening hips, height increase.

row.subject: Science
row.subtopic: Ray Diagrams for Mirrors and Lenses
row.questionText:
Draw the ray diagram in each case to show the position, nature of image formed when the object is placed:
a. at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror
b. within focal length of a convex lens
c. between pole and focus of concave mirror
d. in front of concave lens
e. in front of convex mirror
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Object at C of a concave mirror: image is formed at C itself; real, inverted and of the same size as the object (ray diagram).
[1 mark] (b) Object within the focal length of a convex lens (between O and F1): image is virtual, erect, magnified and on the same side as the object (ray diagram).
[1 mark] (c) Object between pole P and focus F of a concave mirror: image is formed behind the mirror; virtual, erect and magnified (ray diagram).
[1 mark] (d) Object in front of a concave lens: image is always virtual, erect, diminished, formed between the optical centre O and focus F1 on the same side as the object (ray diagram).
[1 mark] (e) Object in front of a convex mirror: image is always virtual, erect, diminished, formed behind the mirror between the pole P and focus F (ray diagram).
row.finalAnswer: (a) at C: real, inverted, same size; (b) virtual, erect, magnified, same side; (c) virtual, erect, magnified, behind mirror; (d) virtual, erect, diminished, between O and F1; (e) virtual, erect, diminished, between P and F behind the mirror.
row.diagramDescription: Five ray diagrams: (a) object at C of a concave mirror giving a real, inverted, same-size image at C; (b) object within the focal length of a convex lens giving a virtual, erect, magnified image on the same side; (c) object between P and F of a concave mirror giving a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror; (d) object in front of a concave lens giving a virtual, erect, diminished image between O and F1; (e) object in front of a convex mirror giving a virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F behind the mirror.

row.subject: Science
row.questionText:
Draw the ray diagram in each case to show the position and nature of image formed when the object is placed:
(a) at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror
(b) within focal length of a convex lens
(c) between pole and focus of concave mirror
(d) in front of concave lens
(e) in front of convex mirror
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (a) Concave mirror, object at C: image at C, real, inverted and of the same size.
[1 mark] (b) Convex lens, object within the focal length: image on the same side as the object, virtual, erect and magnified.
[1 mark] (c) Concave mirror, object between P and F: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect and magnified.
[1 mark] (d) Concave lens, object in front: image between the optical centre and F on the object side, virtual, erect and diminished.
[1 mark] (e) Convex mirror, object in front: image between P and F behind the mirror, virtual, erect and diminished.
row.finalAnswer: Five standard ray diagrams with the stated image positions and natures.
row.diagramDescription: Five diagrams: (a) concave mirror, object at C - real, inverted, same-size image at C; (b) convex lens, object between O and F1 - virtual, erect, magnified image on the same side; (c) concave mirror, object between P and F - virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror; (d) concave lens - virtual, erect, diminished image between O and F1 on the object side; (e) convex mirror - virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F behind the mirror.

row.questionText: What is the nature of the image formed by a convex lens if the magnification produced by the convex lens is +3?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Positive magnification means the image is virtual and erect
[1 mark] Magnitude 3 is greater than 1, so the image is magnified 3 times; this happens when the object is between the optical centre and the focus

row.questionText: What is the nature of the image formed by a convex lens if the magnification produced by the convex lens is -0.5?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Negative magnification means the image is real and inverted
[1 mark] Magnitude 0.5 is less than 1, so the image is diminished; this happens when the object is placed beyond 2F
